title: The perfume (Mark 14:3–9)
hook: a woman breaks a jar worth a year's wages over his head and he defends her
carry: she has done a beautiful thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tables overturned in the Temple courts. Your line was a house of prayer. What space did you clear? Day fifty-nine. Two days before the Passover, in Bethany.

A dinner in Bethany, at the house of a man called Simon the leper. Jesus is reclining at the table with friends. Everyone knows the religious authorities are looking for a way to arrest him. The air is heavy. And a woman walks in holding a small alabaster jar. Inside is pure nard, a perfume made from a plant that grows far away in the Himalayas. It's worth, someone says, more than three hundred denarii. Nearly a year's wages. And she doesn't open it. She breaks it. Snaps the neck of the jar, and pours the whole thing over his head. The smell fills the room. Nobody can pretend it didn't happen. Today: the perfume.
screen: `A DINNER IN BETHANY.` → `AN ALABASTER JAR OF NARD.` → `SHE BREAKS IT OVER HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Some of the guests are furious. Why this waste? That could have been sold, and the money given to the poor. And they scold her. It sounds like a good point. It's the kind of thing we'd say. But Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me." The Greek is kalon ergon, and kalon means both good and beautiful. That's why many modern translations say, she has done a beautiful thing. He says: you'll always have the poor with you, and you can help them whenever you want. That's not dismissing the poor; he's echoing the Law of Moses, which says there will always be poor people, so open your hand to them. But me, he says, you won't always have. She has done what she could. She's anointed my body ahead of time, for burial. She understood what was coming when the others didn't. And then one of the most astonishing promises in the Gospels: "wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done, shall be told for a memorial of her." And here we are, telling it. Yet Mark never gives her name. John tells a similar story and says it was Mary of Bethany, Martha's sister. For centuries in the West, after a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great, she was also thought to be Mary Magdalene. The Church's calendar now treats them as separate women. One more thing: anointing someone's head was what you did for a king. Messiah means anointed one. She's the one who does it.
screen: `WHY THIS WASTE?` · `KALON — GOOD AND BEAUTIFUL.` · `ANOINTED AHEAD, FOR BURIAL.` · `TOLD WHEREVER THE GOSPEL GOES.` · then, large: `SHE HATH WROUGHT A GOOD WORK UPON ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something lavishly. Settle and breathe. We're good at giving the sensible amount. The polite gift, the right-sized favor. Think of one person who deserves more than sensible. Someone who's carrying something heavy right now. What could you give them that's a little extravagant? Your whole evening. A long letter. Real attention, with the phone in another room. Picture breaking the jar. If you pray, you can offer God something lavish too: time, or thanks. The bell holds the time.
The perfume. A jar broken over his head, a room full of scent, and a woman remembered wherever the story is told. Today's word.
Your line: she has done a beautiful thing. Today, give one gift that's a little more than sensible. Day fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the anointing at Bethany in the Passion read on Palm Sunday in the year of Mark, and the Church's anointings with holy oils, at baptism, confirmation and ordination, echo the meaning of the word Christ, the anointed one.

original.note: Greek: a good work, a beautiful work. Kalon means both, which is why translations differ.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman wastes expensive perfume on Jesus.
what it means: she anoints him for burial when no one else understands what's coming, and he promises the world will remember her.
what a scholar hears: kalon ergon, good or beautiful. anointing the head was for kings, and Messiah means anointed one.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 14:6 and 14:9 given from memory; confirm.
The carry 'she has done a beautiful thing' follows modern translations of kalon ergon; the Douay-Rheims 'a good work' is quoted and the difference explained. Confirm.
Nard (spikenard) from the Himalayan region: standard; three hundred denarii as 'nearly a year's wages': standard.

Gregory the Great's Homily 33 (591) identified the anointing woman with Mary Magdalene; the 1969 General Roman Calendar revision treated Mary Magdalene separately. Confirm phrasing ('the Church's calendar now treats them as separate women').
'You'll always have the poor' is linked to Deuteronomy 15:11; confirm this reading is fairly put.
